name: Yusuf Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on a maintenance and storm crew for a mid-size power company that covers the suburbs and the farms past them. Day to day it's planned work, replacing old transformers, changing out insulators, clearing lines, and then whenever there's a storm everything stops and we go out until it's fixed. I'm the newest on the crew and still learning, so I do a lot of rigging and ground work. I like the brotherhood of it, the way the crew looks out for each other.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's going on outside of work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm getting married next summer, to Amira, she's a primary school teacher. We've been saving for the wedding and for a house deposit, so we've got about ten months of my pay put aside, plus the deposit fund. I use the AI chatbot sometimes, mainly to check exam questions, and once to help with a toast for my brother's wedding. My faith and my family come first, then the job, and the job's good to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people got carried away again. At the depot we'd laugh about it. I'd tell my dad the same thing he told me years ago: a man with a trade is never stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the plan goes ahead. Wedding next summer, house the year after, kids after that, and the work stays steady. The pay's good too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the apprenticeship, keep going out on every storm call for the overtime, and keep putting money aside for the house. We'd book the wedding hall in January like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices. Even with good pay, they're high round here. We might need to look a bit further out, near Amira's parents, which would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you turn to if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Amira's dad has been a builder for thirty years and he'd help us find something. My uncle too.

say: I'd say people **got carried away** again.
I'd repeat my dad's line that a man with **a trade** is never stuck.
think: Privately, the **wedding and house plan** goes ahead on schedule.
The storm and maintenance work stays **steady** and well paid.
do: Keep doing the **apprenticeship** and every storm call for overtime.
Book the **wedding hall** in January as planned.
S0.quote: Wedding next summer, house the year after, kids after that, and the work stays steady.
fieldNote: His plans revolve around **marriage and family**, in a set order.
His worry is **house prices**, not technology, and he'd look further out.
He'd lean on **family** first, especially his builder father-in-law.

steps.text: Take every storm call for the overtime pay
Book the wedding hall in January
Keep adding to the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to do what makes sense, and AI is part of that now. I'd tell the guys at the depot to learn it, not fight it. Online I wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. The power company would cut office jobs and maybe review crews too, and I'm the last one hired. I don't think they'd cut lineworkers, but I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new system comes in, once the senior guys are using it. I'd still go ahead with the wedding, but maybe smaller, and push the house back a few months. I'd also ask the foreman what I can do to be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fewer guests, or a simpler venue. Amira would be disappointed, but she'd understand. Our families would still be there, that's what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the foreman tell you, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show up early, never complain on a storm call, and know your knots. He says that every week anyway.

say: I'd say companies must **do what makes sense**.
I'd tell the depot to **learn it**, not fight it.
think: Privately, he's the **last one hired**, which worries him a little.
He doesn't expect **lineworker cuts**, but would feel the pressure.
do: Learn the **new system** once senior crew use it.
Have a **smaller wedding** and push the house back months.
Ask the **foreman** how to be the one they keep.
feel: He feels **uneasy**: not scared, just watching.
S1.quote: The power company would cut office jobs and maybe review crews too, and I'm the last one hired.
fieldNote: His **free-market** views make him accept company decisions without blame.
Being **last hired** on the crew is his main exposure.
He'd **trim the wedding** before touching savings or family priorities.

steps.text: Learn the new work-order system once senior crew use it
Cut the wedding guest list and pick a simpler venue
Ask the foreman what makes an apprentice worth keeping

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle well, and families are going to pay for it. I'd still say people need to work, not wait for handouts. At church we'd be praying about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot. The office goes in 2028, but the robots for our work come around 2031, right when we'd have a mortgage and maybe a baby. I'd have three years to get ready, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding small and hold off on the house completely. I'd look at a technical diploma in power systems, something more than climbing. And I'd talk to Amira's dad about joining his building firm if line work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We've got savings, so we're okay for a while, but I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait, and we keep the deposit safe. She'd want the house, and so would I, but I'd rather rent a bit longer than lose the house we saved for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at building work. Wouldn't robots come for that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I suppose I'd still rather be near family and learning something real. But you're right, it's not a sure thing.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families will pay for it.
I'd insist people need **to work**, not wait for handouts.
think: Privately, robots by **2031** arrive as he'd have a mortgage and baby.
do: Keep the **wedding small** and hold off the house completely.
Look at a **power systems diploma** beyond climbing.
Ask his future **father-in-law** about building work.
feel: He feels **anxious** but okay for a while with savings.
S2.quote: I'd rather rent a bit longer than lose the house we saved for.
fieldNote: His fear is tied to **family timing**: mortgage and baby.
He admits his **fallback** may not be safe either.

steps.text: Hold off buying a house and keep the deposit safe
Enrol in a power systems technical diploma
Ask his future father-in-law about joining the building firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and people should take it seriously. Get a trade, learn new skills, look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be a journeyman, married, maybe with a house. Robots at 2034 would still hit, but I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the wedding as planned next summer, buy a smaller house, and start the diploma next year. I'd keep saving the way we do now, a set amount every payday. Amira's dad would help us look at houses near his place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but we'd be okay, I think, with the savings and family around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a smaller house mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two bedrooms instead of three. Room for one kid, and we'd move later if we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep apprenticeships going and help people retrain, because people want to work, not just get cheques. That's how my family has always seen it.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning.
I'd tell people to get **a trade** and look after their family.
think: Privately, he'd be a **journeyman** and married by 2031.
Robots at **2034** still hit, but he'd have time.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** next summer as planned.
Buy a **smaller house** near his future in-laws.
Start the **power systems diploma** next year.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but believes they'd be okay.
S3.quote: Keep apprenticeships going and help people retrain, because people want to work, not just get cheques.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **keep the wedding** and still buy a home.
He wants government to fund **retraining**, not hand out cheques.
He'd scale down to a **two-bedroom** house with room for one child.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Buy a two-bedroom house instead of three
Start the power systems diploma next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody has an excuse. Work hard, learn what's needed, and you'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I'm happiest with. By 2036 I'd be well into my career, married, kids, a house. Robots around 2039 would be something to plan for slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with everything: wedding, house, kids. I'd do the diploma in a few years, once I've got my ticket. And I'd keep saving every payday, like my dad taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the plateau, really, but with a long warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, and learn the new stuff too. Don't be scared of it, but don't trust it blindly either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the young apprentices coming after me get a chance. If companies stop training apprentices, the trade dies anyway.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so nobody has an excuse.
I'd tell people to **work hard** and learn what's needed.
think: Privately, this is the one he's **happiest with**, with career and family settled.
Robots around **2039** can be planned for slowly, over years.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding, house and kids**.
Do the **diploma** in a few years.
feel: He feels **calm**, like the plateau but with long warning.
S4.quote: If companies stop training apprentices, the trade dies anyway.
fieldNote: He worries more about **future apprentices** than himself.
Ten years restores his **full family plan**.
He'd teach his kids to **learn new tools** but not trust them blindly.

steps.text: Go ahead with the wedding, house and children
Take the power systems diploma in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It lands right when we'd be starting a family. What would help is the company keeping apprentices on and paying for diplomas, and our families around us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith, maybe. A lot of us at the depot lean on church when things get hard. That would matter more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: A lot of us at the depot lean on church when things get hard.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old apprentice** on a maintenance and storm crew for a mid-size utility.
He's **getting married** next summer and saving for a house deposit.
He uses **AI now and then** and accepts company decisions as part of a free market.
He's calm or uneasy in slow pictures but **anxious** when robots arrive by 2031.
His **family plans** shift with how much warning there is.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands right as he'd be **starting a family**.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping **apprentices** and paying for diplomas, and **family** around him.
